caption:
Wells Fargo's new online banking terms take effect November 24, and they say using an AI agent on your account is "AT YOUR OWN RISK."
Anything the agent does counts as if you did it, and the bank says it does not watch what agents do.
JPMorgan, Citi, Schwab and Bank of America are also pushing outside AI agents out or putting the risk on customers.

Would you let an AI agent touch your bank account?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Wells Fargo, American Banker, AIM Media House · Photo: American Banker
threads_text: Starting November 24, Wells Fargo's terms say any AI agent you let into your account acts as you, at your own risk, and the bank does not monitor it. Other big banks are blocking outside agents outright. Would you trust an AI agent with your bank login?

paragraphs.text: Wells Fargo's updated Online Access Agreement takes effect on November 24, 2026, and it adds a section on third-party artificial intelligence agents. According to the bank's own notice of the update, a third-party AI tool is not operated by Wells Fargo, and requests it makes may be treated as if they came directly from the customer.

The new Section 15 defines an AI agent broadly, as any software that acts on behalf of a person or entity, whether autonomously or not, according to AIM Media House, which quoted the agreement. The same section says the use of any AI agent is at the customer's own risk, a line the agreement prints in capital letters.
What the terms ask of customers

Under the terms, instructions and transactions coming from a customer's agent are deemed to be initiated and authorized by the customer without further verification. The bank also states that it does not monitor, screen or review what AI agents do in an account, AIM Media House reported.

Customers who revoke an agent's access must keep evidence of that revocation and provide it to the bank on request, according to American Banker and AIM Media House. They remain responsible for the agent's activity until they notify the bank, and the bank may require agents to be registered. Wells Fargo has not issued a public statement explaining the change, AIM Media House said.

The law firm Hunton Andrews Kurth noted that Wells Fargo did not block agents outright. Instead, it rewrote its online access terms so the risk of using an agent sits with the customer, and it reserved the right to limit or end agent access at any time.
Other banks take a harder line

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said on the bank's October 13 earnings call that it would not let outside agents, including Meta's Muse, act inside customer accounts, according to Hunton Andrews Kurth. Chase's updated Digital Services Agreement, effective January 1, 2027, says a customer who gives an agent access authorizes everything the agent does. Chief financial officer Jeremy Barnum said customers who share credentials with an external agent bear the risk, AIM Media House reported.

Citigroup said it does not permit third-party AI agents or assistants to log into customer accounts, while still allowing limited read-only access through some open banking providers. Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said the firm blocks unauthorized agents, including Muse, that try to move client money 10 to 20 times a week, according to Hunton Andrews Kurth.

Bank of America sent customers an email warning them against sharing login details with AI tools that offer to act on their behalf, and telling them they are responsible for activity that results from such access, according to AIM Media House, which cited TechCrunch.

Federal Regulation E protects consumers against unauthorized electronic transfers. AIM Media House noted that when a customer has handed credentials to another party, that protection may not apply in the same way, and that no court or regulator has ruled on the question for AI agents. Hunton Andrews Kurth said guidance on authorization and liability may follow.

The bank terms show how the industry is handling agents that can log in and move money before any common rules exist. Rather than wait for regulators, banks are either shutting outside agents out or writing contracts that place the loss on the customer. For consumers, the practical effect is that a mistake by an agent with full login access may be treated as their own instruction.

Chase's new agreement takes effect on January 1, 2027, and any guidance from US regulators on whether Regulation E covers transfers made by AI agents would decide who pays when an agent gets a payment wrong.
